entries.meaning: Coined name of an imaginary Celtic priestess in Bellini's opera Norma (1831). Sometimes explained as Latin norma (“pattern, model”), or as a feminine form of Norman.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Norman, from Old English Norman (a variant of Norþman) and Old French Normant. It is certain that the word is derived from the base of the Germanic words for north and the Germanic base of the words for man. However, given the frequent movement of Germanic groups especially into and out of Britain in the post-classical world, it is unclear in what tongue it came to be used first.
entries.note: A male given name from Old English used in the Middle Ages and revived in the 19th century.
entries.origin: Old English used in the Middle Ages and revived in the 19th century

entries.meaning: An Anglo-Norman surname, from Old French norreis (“a northerner, a migrant from the north”). More at French norois.

entries.meaning: From Old English norþ (“north”) + tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”). The parish in New Brunswick is named after Norton, Massachusetts.

entries.meaning: English and Scottish surname of Norman origin meaning "northern town," shortened from Normanville, equivalent to Norman + -ville.
